content: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a significant global health issue. Medicinal herbs are increasingly being explored as potential treatments for this condition. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of medicinal herbs in treating HCV infection. To conduct this evaluation, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, The Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field, The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, and Chinese and Japanese databases, as of February 2001. Additionally, five Chinese journals and one Japanese journal were manually searched. No restrictions were placed on language. The study included randomized clinical trials that compared medicinal herbs to placebo, no intervention, general non-specific treatments, other herbal medicines, or standard treatments such as interferon and/or ribavirin. Trials that combined medicinal herbs with interferon and/or ribavirin and compared them to interferon and/or ribavirin alone were also included. Two independent authors extracted data from the trials, and the methodological quality of the studies was assessed using criteria such as allocation sequence generation, allocation concealment, double blinding, and the Jadad scale. The results were presented as relative risks or weighted mean differences, both with 95% confidence intervals. The analysis included ten randomized trials involving 517 patients, most of whom had chronic hepatitis C. These trials evaluated ten different medicinal herbs against various control interventions, including placebo, interferon, and other herbs. The methodological quality was deemed adequate in four trials and inadequate in six trials. When compared to placebo in four trials, none of the medicinal herbs demonstrated significant effects on clearing serum HCV RNA, anti-HCV antibodies, or improving serum liver enzyme levels. However, one short-term trial using a silybin preparation showed a significant reduction in serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase (GGT) activities. The herbal compound Bing Gan Tang, when combined with interferon-alpha, showed significantly better outcomes in clearing serum HCV RNA (relative risk 2.54; 95% confidence interval 1.43 to 4.49) and normalizing serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (relative risk 2.54; 95% confidence interval 1.43 to 4.49) compared to interferon-alpha monotherapy. Similarly, the herbal compound Yi Zhu decoction demonstrated significant effects in clearing serum HCV RNA and normalizing ALT levels when compared to glycyrrhizin plus ribavirin. Yi Er Gan Tang was found to significantly normalize serum ALT levels compared to silymarin plus glucurolactone. However, no significant efficacy was observed for the other herbs examined in the trials. Adverse events were associated with the use of these medicinal herbs. In conclusion, there is no robust evidence to support the efficacy of any medicinal herbs for the treatment of HCV infection. Therefore, medicinal herbs should not be used for HCV infection outside the context of randomized clinical trials.
